ayanamsa gives the mean and true ayanamsa of a definition at an instant read as a chart reads its own: on the engine's time basis, or on a pinned ΔT, and refused outside EPHEMERIS_SPAN. Its true value is the mean plus the engine's nutation in longitude, IAU 2000B with all 77 of its terms, which cancels from sidereal longitudes. siderealChart gives a chart's bodies, angles and cusps as sidereal longitudes, with the ayanamsa at the chart's instant on the chart's own ΔT clock.

@zodiacs/engine/vedic's ayanamsa reads its instant as a chart reads its own: options.timeScale names the scale, "utc" (the default), "ut1" or "tt", as BirthInput.timeScale does, and options.deltaT fixes ΔT (TT − UT1) in seconds, as BirthInput.deltaT does, the engine's time basis giving it when absent. The value records the ΔT the instant was read with (the time basis's, or the pin), timeScale, the same record of how the instant became UT1 and TT that a chart carries, and utc, the instant as given in ISO 8601 on the scale timeScale.input names, as ChartInput.utc is named, so a UT1 or TT reading is written with a Z. A sidereal longitude made from an ayanamsa read on UT1 or TT (a chart given on either) carries in utc the UTC instant of its time basis, as the timing entry reads the chart. A caller's ayanamsa (userAyanamsa) takes its epoch as { julianDateTT }, a TT Julian date within the Date range, or as a UTC instant, a Date or an ISO 8601 string, read on the engine's time basis.
birthWindow labels its results WINDOW_VERIFICATION, "sampled at one-second resolution": they are checked against dense sampling, not proven.

In @zodiacs/engine/geo a birthplace longitude, in degrees east, makes the birthplace's own mean time (longitude × 240 s) replace the zone's local mean time before the zone's local mean time era ended: resolveLocalToUtc takes it as its longitude option, resolveLocalBirth uses the birth's longitude for it as well as for the chart, and moonSignCandidates' longitude option reads a date's midnights the same way, through resolveLocalToUtc. A resolution's localMeanTime is set exactly where the birthplace's own mean time read the wall time, and is null otherwise.
chart() in @zodiacs/engine/calc gives, as its chart, the chart natalChart() gives for the same instant (read to the nearest millisecond), place, settings and ΔT, in the tropical zodiac.

The candidates before 1.0 that had the calc entry, 0.1.1-rc.16 and rc.17, wrote calc receipts with the schema id "zodiacs.calc-receipt.draft-v1", whose requests name a Julian date's scale in capitals and houses()'s house system as system; from 1.0 (first written by 1.0.0-rc.1, and so by 1.0.0) the id is CALC_RECEIPT_SCHEMA, "zodiacs.calc-receipt.v1", and its requests are in 1.0's vocabulary, lowercase scales and houseSystem.

@zodiacs/engine/calc reads an instant given as an ISO 8601 string or a Date as UTC on the engine's time basis, as positions() and natalChart() read one, or a Julian date on a named time scale ("utc", "ut1" or "tt"); a deltaT fixes ΔT = TT − UT1, in seconds, in place of the time basis's: UT1 still comes from the instant (UTC plus IERS UT1 − UTC from 1972), and TT = UT1 + ΔT.

A chart records the ΔT (TT − UT1) it was computed with, with its 1-σ band and its source: the model zodiacs-deltat/1, "iers-utc/1" (the leap seconds and IERS UT1 − UTC), or a caller's pin. Each ΔT names the table it came from (table, tableDigest): DELTA_T_TABLE's for the model, the UT1 table's for iers-utc/1; a pin's sigma, table and tableDigest are null. BirthInput.deltaT fixes ΔT at that many seconds instead of the engine's time basis, while UT1 still comes from the instant, and the chart then reports deltaT.model "pinned". A chart's timeScale records how its instant became UT1, from which the angles take the Earth's rotation, and TT, at which the positions are computed. chartDeclinations reports the ΔT it evaluated on the chart's clock to obtain the true obliquity.

@zodiacs/engine/houses' coAscendants returns the four points Swiss Ephemeris returns in ascmc[4] to ascmc[7]: the equatorial ascendant, Koch's co-ascendant, Munkasey's co-ascendant and Munkasey's polar ascendant, each in degrees in [0, 360).

The doc comment of coAscendants says each co-ascendant is taken as the formula gives it, so that inside the polar circle, and for Munkasey's co-ascendant within 90° − ε of the equator, it can lie west of the meridian and is not turned east. That holds of the equatorial ascendant, Koch's co-ascendant and the polar ascendant; but Munkasey's co-ascendant is the ascendant at the colatitude, so it can lie west only where the colatitude is inside the polar circle, within ε, about 23.44°, of the equator, not within 90° − ε.

resolution.note: The comment should say within ε of the equator. F-89: statements in engine 1.0.0's README, NOTICE, LICENSING and doc comments that the claims ledger found inaccurate; correct them in the engine's next release, and the reference served here follows when it is regenerated for that release.

claims.statement: findLongitudeCrossings is findLongitudeCrossingsWith, the engine's one crossing solver, run on the engine's own apparent geocentric longitudes, with its conventions: in the window (from, to] a root exactly at from is not reported and one exactly at to is, a sample exactly on the target is reported once, and both crossings around a station that falls between two samples are found and kept. The search assumes smooth motion with at most one station in two steps; it is tested, not proven complete.

The dasha functions of @zodiacs/engine/vedic count a dasha year as 365.25 days ("julian", the default), 365.2422 days ("tropical") or the 360-day savana year ("savana"), the lengths DASHA_YEAR_DAYS exports; any other yearLength is refused.

The doc comment of ChartInput.deltaT says a chart uses the engine's model when no ΔT is pinned. Without a pin a chart's ΔT comes from the engine's time basis: iers-utc/1, from the leap seconds and IERS UT1 − UTC, from 1972-01-01 to 2027-10-02, and the model zodiacs-deltat/1 only outside that span.

resolution.note: The comment should say the engine's time basis, as BirthInput.deltaT's does. F-89: statements in engine 1.0.0's README, NOTICE, LICENSING and doc comments that the claims ledger found inaccurate; correct them in the engine's next release, and the reference served here follows when it is regenerated for that release.

claims.statement: A ΔT's segment says where it came from: one of the ΔT model's segments ("long-term", "reconstructed", "observed", "predicted" or "extrapolated"), "pinned" for a caller's pin, or, on the IERS basis (model "iers-utc/1"), the source of its UT1 − UTC, "observed" or "predicted". The value "fallback", the IERS basis with UT1 − UTC taken as 0 ± 0.9 s past the table's ends, was recorded only by rc.15's first cut, whose receipts carry it; later releases do not give it, and the receipt codec still accepts it so that those records stay readable.

@zodiacs/engine 1.0.0's /crossings and /deltat are public standalone entry points whose exports the root entry point also re-exports, and the API reference includes them; /internal and /internal/math are compatibility entries for the Zodiacs site, outside the package's public API promise, which may change without notice, and the reference leaves them out.

EPHEMERIS_SPAN is the span of Terrestrial Time over which the ephemeris is evaluated at all: J2000 ± 730,000 days of TT, 0001-04-30T12:00 to 3998-09-03T12:00 TT, the years astronomy-engine 2.1.19, the exact version the engine depends on, itself tabulates. Every instant a calculation evaluates, the instant and each of its speed samples, must lie inside it on the calculation's own ΔT clock (its time basis or a pin), or the call throws a RangeError; with the model ΔT, instants from 0001-05-01T00:00Z to 3998-09-02T00:00Z are always inside.

In @zodiacs/engine/geo's Gregorian adoption table (GREGORIAN_ADOPTION), each row's note gives the other regions the sources date, by their first New Style days, and where the sources disagree; a date in a note is tzdb's (the calendars file of IANA tzdata 2025c, which quotes Grotefend's 1941 edition) unless another source, Grotefend 1891 or 1898, is named.

@zodiacs/engine/geo reads a local date in the calendar its calendar option names, "gregorian" by default or "julian" (Old Style), converting a Julian date through the Julian Day Number to the proleptic Gregorian date before resolving the wall time; any other calendar is refused.

resolveLocalBirth and resolveBirth in @zodiacs/engine/geo read an omitted birth time as 12:00 local wall time; a time may be omitted only when timeKnown is false or absent (timeKnown true without a time is refused), and the reference is then "local-noon".

@zodiacs/engine/geo's resolveLocalToUtc flags a skipped wall time "dst-gap" and a repeated one "dst-fold" whatever caused the jump (the dst- names are kept for compatibility; jump.cause gives the cause), and flags "lmt" where a local mean time clock read the wall time. A transition's cause, "dst", "legal-change" or "date-line", comes from the tzdb record: an offset change of 12 hours or more is a date-line move, a change of the zone line's standard offset a legal change, and a change of the daylight-saving part alone daylight saving.
MEAN_LUNAR_INCLINATION, the Moon's mean orbital inclination to the ecliptic that the engine's mean-orbit point formulas use, is 5.1453964°, that is 5°08′43.4″.

moonPhase is a high-precision Moon phase derived from the same positions as charts: its angle is the apparent geocentric longitude of the Moon less that of the Sun, from the same ephemeris functions a chart's bodies come from, which the engine's tests hold within 0.01° of JPL Horizons.

moonSignCandidates gives the Moon signs possible over a civil date. With a timeZone the date runs from local midnight to local midnight, read as resolveLocalToUtc (@zodiacs/engine/geo) reads them, so before 1970 its prepareLocalTime must be awaited first or the call throws geo's ZoneHistoryNotLoadedError, an Error and not a RangeError. Without one the date is read in every time zone, from 00:00 at UTC+14 to 24:00 at UTC−12, and sign is set only when the Moon held one sign over that whole span.

moonSignCandidates reads a date in the IANA zone its timeZone option names, from local midnight to the millisecond before the next, as resolveLocalToUtc reads them; without timeZone it reads the date in every time zone, from 00:00 at UTC+14 to 24:00 at UTC−12 (EVERY_ZONE_OFFSETS), and reports timeZone as null.

A natal record's result holds the chart's bodies, angles, houses and aspects and, from later conventions sets, its ΔT (from the rc.8 set on) and its time scale, how the instant became UT1 and TT (from the time-basis set, rc.15's, on): createNatalEnvelope writes all six, and the codec requires deltaT and timeScale where the record's conventions set names them and refuses them under an earlier set.

natalReplayInput replays a natal record from the request and instant it recorded: the recorded UTC instant, with its time scale and any pinned ΔT, and the requested house system, never the whole-sign houses a polar fallback put in its place, and never a local time resolved again on today's tzdb.

The doc comment of placidusCusps says the iteration settles to 1e-9° within 64 steps except within about 1e-8° of the polar limit near the sidereal times at which a cusp's right ascension reaches 90° or 270°, where it needs up to 63 steps and asin's rounding moves each step by about the tolerance. The 64-step cap, the tolerance, the bisection fallback and the band below the limit are in the code and its tests; the figure of 63 steps and the size of the rounding are not recorded by any committed test or evidence.

resolution.note: Record the step count near the limit in a test, or drop the figure. F-89: statements in engine 1.0.0's README, NOTICE, LICENSING and doc comments that the claims ledger found inaccurate; correct them in the engine's next release, and the reference served here follows when it is regenerated for that release.

claims.statement: Where Placidus and Koch are undefined, inside the polar circle, the engine falls back to whole-sign houses (POLAR_FALLBACK) while Swiss Ephemeris falls back to Porphyry; asked for "porphyry", the engine computes that system at any latitude, the polar circle included, with no fallback.

progressedInstant maps elapsed life to the instant whose positions are progressed: one tropical year of 365.2422 days after birth advances one day of 86,400,000 ms, both counted in UTC milliseconds as Date counts them (no leap seconds), not in ephemeris days. progressedBodies gives the positions() rows at that instant, whose speed remains the ephemeris rate in degrees per day there, a central difference over ±0.001 day (±0.25 day for the nodes), and so is numerically also degrees per tropical year of life, not degrees per lived day.

createNatalEnvelope keeps sourceInstant, the caller's original ISO 8601 spelling, only after checking that it parses to the receipt's instant, and infers no zone or offset meaning from it; a captured local resolution is checked arithmetically (the wall time plus any gap shift less the offset must give the instant, under the fixed fold and gap policy, with the flags, calendar and transition consistent) without consulting the host's Intl or any time-zone database.

REFERENCE_SPAN, from 1800-01-01T00:00Z up to but not including 2200-01-01T00:00Z, is the span over which the engine's positions have been compared with an independent ephemeris. calc() and the other functions of @zodiacs/engine/calc compute an instant only if its UT1 and its TT both lie in that span (CALC_SPAN), refusing any other as out-of-range, while positions() and natalChart() compute outside it with the outside-reference-span flag; a techniques result carries that flag when the ephemeris was read outside 1800–2200.
SIDEREAL_TIME_RATE, the rate of sidereal time by which @zodiacs/engine/houses turns derivatives with respect to the RAMC into speeds per day, is 360.98564736629 degrees of RAMC per day of UT1.

@zodiacs/engine/sky takes the refraction at the horizon as 34′ (STANDARD_REFRACTION_ARCMIN, the US Naval Observatory's figure in its Rise, Set, and Twilight Definitions) under refraction "standard", the default, and as 0 under "none", recording it in conventions.refractionArcmin as 34 or 0; it takes a disc's semi-diameter from SKY_RADII_KM, the Sun's radius of 696,000 km, which subtends 959.64″ at 1 au, and the Moon's IAU mean radius, 1,737.4 km; and skyEventsOn's day runs on a clock utcOffsetMinutes east of UTC, by default the observer's local mean time, longitude × 4 minutes.

In @zodiacs/engine/sky a calendar date is read on a clock utcOffsetMinutes east of UTC, by default the observer's local mean time (4 minutes per degree of east longitude). skyEventsOn gives skyEvents over that one day; planetaryHours gives the planetary day that begins at the Sun's first rise on the date: the day's ruler, sunrise, sunset, the next sunrise and the 24 hours.

By convention, declinationsForBodies never flags a supplied row labelled exactly "Sun" as out of bounds while its ecliptic latitude is within SUN_BOUND_LATITUDE, 0.001° (3.6″). The flag could not say which way the real Sun lies: the real Sun does pass the bound at about half of all solstices (402 of the 800 from 1800 to 2199, by ERFA), by up to about 1.1″, but the ephemeris's solar declination is off by up to about 2.7″ near the present (against DE440s, 1850 to 2150) and its solar latitude by tens of arcseconds far from it (−68″ at the June solstice of year 2, +26″ at that of 3902), more than the effect.

positions(date) returns the Sun, the Moon, eight planets and the true lunar nodes. natalChart(birth) adds natal aspects and, when coordinates are present, angles and houses in any of thirteen systems. chartPoints(natal) returns the mean node and Black Moon Lilith and, with a birth time and place, the Vertex, the East Point, the chart's sect and seven lots. findConfiguredAspects(bodies, policy) finds aspects under an explicit policy from createAspectPolicy, minor and custom angles included. chartDeclinations(natal) derives right ascension, declination, parallel aspects and out-of-bounds flags on the chart's clock. progressedInstant(birthUtc, target) maps each elapsed tropical year of life to one day after birth, and progressedBodies(birthUtc, target) returns the twelve ordinary position rows at that instant. transits(natal, date) returns a sky snapshot and moving-to-natal aspects; synastry(a, b) inter-chart aspects and element and modality balances; moonPhase(date) the elongation, the illuminated fraction and the phase name; saturnReturn(birth) the exact-pass seasons through roughly age 92. findLongitudeCrossings(body, longitude, from, to) returns the instants a body crosses a longitude, and searchLongitudeCrossings does the same under a sample budget. The optional entry points provide: @zodiacs/engine/crossings, the same solver for a caller's own longitude function, without the ephemeris; @zodiacs/engine/geo, IANA local-time resolution, Julian calendar dates and a client for a separately hosted, sharded GeoNames index; @zodiacs/engine/techniques, solar and lunar returns, composite and Davison charts, the void-of-course Moon, aspect patterns, essential dignities and the Moon signs possible over a date; @zodiacs/engine/timing, profections, firdaria, zodiacal releasing, solar arc directions and planetary returns; @zodiacs/engine/houses, the house position of a body with ecliptic latitude in each house system, the co-ascendants and the polar ascendant, and the speeds of the cusps and the angles, importing no ephemeris and no module of the root entry; @zodiacs/engine/vedic, the sidereal zodiac: ayanamsas, sidereal charts, nakshatras, vargas, KP sub-lords and dashas; @zodiacs/engine/sky, rise, set and transit times for an observer and planetary hours; and @zodiacs/engine/window, the partition of a birth-time window into cells within which the chart's signs, houses and aspects are constant.

A chart records in timeScale how its instant became UT1 and TT: basis "iers" where TT came from the leap seconds (TT = UTC + (TAI − UTC) + 32.184 s) and UT1 from IERS UT1 − UTC, "delta-t" where the civil instant was read as UT1 and TT came from the ΔT model, and "pinned" where the caller fixed ΔT. Its leapSeconds is null wherever TT did not come from the leap seconds, and its ut1MinusUtc is the UT1 − UTC actually used: IERS observed or predicted from the table, or 0 within ±0.9 s ("fallback") outside it.

evidence.match: var fallback = () => ({ seconds: 0, sigma: UT1_FALLBACK_BAND, source: "fallback" });

claims.statement: In @zodiacs/engine/timing, profection year n runs from the n-th solar return (the apparent Sun back on its natal longitude; the birth for n = 0) to the next, found on the engine's ephemeris from the chart's birth as a UTC instant on the engine's time basis, not on a chart's pinned ΔT; and the solar arc at a target is the Sun of progressedBodies(birthUtc, target) less the natal Sun, both read as UTC instants on the engine's time basis, never on a chart's pinned ΔT.

A result of @zodiacs/engine/timing carries flags as a chart does: "outside-reference-span" when an instant the ephemeris was read at lies outside REFERENCE_SPAN, and "sect-contradicts-altitude" when the result depends on a sect that the Sun's altitude at birth contradicts, which can happen only inside the polar circles.

A caller's ayanamsa in @zodiacs/engine/calc is the counterpart of Swiss Ephemeris's SE_SIDM_USER: the mean ayanamsa value at an epoch, carried from there by precession in a model, or by a fixed rate. Its epoch is read as any instant in a request is: { jd, scale: "tt" } is SE_SIDM_USER's TT epoch, and { jd, scale: "ut1" } its UT epoch (SE_SIDBIT_USER_UT), whose TT comes from the engine's time basis.

In @zodiacs/engine/geo a wall time before 1970 is read on the IANA tzdb 2025c history the package ships, where that history records a local time (where it records none, the host's Intl answers). prepareLocalTime loads what a wall time on a date (YYYY-MM-DD) in a zone needs: up to 1970, the zone's shipped history, one of 16 buckets. Until it has, resolveLocalToUtc throws for a wall time before 1970-01-02, and zoneOffsetAt for an instant before 1970, a ZoneHistoryNotLoadedError: an Error and not a RangeError, because the input is valid, and awaiting prepareLocalTime(date, timeZone) first lets the same call answer. From 1970, and in the fixed Etc zones at every date, the host's Intl answers. zoneOffsetAt is the engine's own offset, the one its wall times use; offsetAt gives the host's Intl offset at a UTC instant, in minutes east, as a cross-check on the host's time-zone data: the two agree from 1970 where the host has tzdata 2025c, and before 1970 they can differ, because Intl does not carry the history the package ships.

The package's frame module (src/frame.ts, built into the ephemeris chunk under dist/) reproduces astronomy-engine's precession function, precession_rot, and the calc entry's reduction module (src/calc-reduce.ts, built into dist/calc.js) reproduces astronomy-engine's function for an observer on the Earth's ellipsoid, terra.
The settings of a public birth input and of resolveBirth are validated once, and the scalar values captured then are the ones used for the calculation or the resolution.

In @zodiacs/engine/calc a measured bound is the largest difference from JPL Horizons (DE441) over 32 instants from 1802 to 2188: a sample maximum, not a limit. What this version does not compute comes back as a typed refusal rather than an exception, such as gravitational deflection (not-in-this-version) or an instant whose UT1 or TT is outside 1800-01-01 to 2200-01-01 (out-of-range), where calc has no comparison to take a bound from; the root entry's functions still compute such an instant and flag it outside-reference-span.

evidence.match: largest difference from JPL Horizons (DE441) over 32 instants from JD 2379457.498125 to 2520522.646618 (TT)
Gravitational light deflection is not modelled in this version.

claims.statement: LICENSING says the bounds of @zodiacs/engine/calc are the largest differences between the package's results and JPL Horizons (DE441) at 32 preregistered instants, and that its barycentre's error is a scan against a Newtonian barycentre checked with Horizons at 88 instants. The barycentre part and most bounds are so; but the bounds of the mean node, the mean south node and Black Moon Lilith, 0.0023″, are differences from those points' definitions computed with ERFA, as the calc preregistration specifies, though the package labels them with the Horizons basis.

resolution.note: LICENSING and the bound labels should name ERFA as the basis of the mean points' bounds. F-89: statements in engine 1.0.0's README, NOTICE, LICENSING and doc comments that the claims ledger found inaccurate; correct them in the engine's next release, and the reference served here follows when it is regenerated for that release.

claims.statement: The calc entry's bounds and its barycentre's error are measurements: the largest differences of the package's own results from NASA JPL Horizons (DE441) responses at 32 instants, and of astronomy-engine's barycentre from a Newtonian barycentre and from Horizons's. They are not coefficients derived from JPL data, and no JPL ephemeris value is in the package.

evidence.match: largest difference from JPL Horizons (DE441) over 32 instants

claims.statement: @zodiacs/engine/calc (dist/calc.js and the chunks it imports) carries the frame bias of the IAU 2000 precession-nutation model, dψ = −0.041775″, dε = −0.0068192″ and dα₀ = −0.0146″, composed as the IERS Conventions (2010), chapter 5, eq. 5.21 (G. Petit and B. Luzum, eds., IERS Technical Note No. 36, 2010), compose it, and the obliquity of J2000.0 of the IAU 2006 precession, 84381.406″.

claims.statement: No value of a JPL ephemeris, and no coefficient fitted to one, is in the package; the NASA JPL Horizons responses the calc entry's bounds were measured against are in docs/evidence/calc-api/, which is not packed.

claims.statement: @zodiacs/engine/calc offers calc, houses, events and chart with one request vocabulary: instants as ISO strings, Dates or { jd, scale: "utc" | "ut1" | "tt" }, read on the engine's time basis as positions() reads them; eight frames, the ecliptic or the equator, each true or mean of date, of J2000.0 or of the ICRS; geocentric, heliocentric, barycentric and topocentric centers; apparent, astrometric or geometric positions with distances and speeds; and the tropical or the sidereal zodiac, with any ayanamsa of @zodiacs/engine/vedic or a caller's own, the counterpart of Swiss Ephemeris's SE_SIDM_USER.

chart.deltaT is { seconds, sigma, model, table, tableDigest, segment }, and chart.timeScale, { input, basis, ut1MinusUtc, leapSeconds }, says how the instant became UT1 and TT. @zodiacs/engine/deltat exports the ΔT model with no dependencies. astronomy-engine keeps one ΔT for its whole module; every engine call leaves the engine's model installed there, and code that calls astronomy-engine directly should install it too with SetDeltaTFunction(deltaT).

LICENSING says the conformance suite's inputs are copies of files from NASA JPL Horizons, the IANA time zone database and the IERS, and that no Swiss Ephemeris code, data file or output is committed, its adapter calling a separately installed pyswisseph whose results are published as verdicts, flags and statistics. The adapter and the publication are so, and no Swiss code or data file is committed; but four of the 24 source files were made by Zodiacs, and one of them, conformance/sources/horizons-24/corpus-tt.json, records Swiss Ephemeris's ΔT for the 24 corpus instants, from which the TT dates sent to Horizons were taken.

resolution.note: conformance/sources/horizons-24/corpus-tt.json records Swiss Ephemeris's ΔT at full precision for the 24 corpus instants, as clock values from which the TT dates sent to Horizons were taken. The owner decides whether those values stay, with LICENSING and the conformance README saying so, or are replaced by an independent ΔT, which would change the Horizons requests.

claims.statement: In the conformance suite under conformance/, Swiss Ephemeris is used only as an instrument: no vector uses it as its arbiter, it is run against the suite like any other engine, and it checks an arbiter's implementation only after the fact.

@zodiacs/engine is ESM-only, has no import-time side effects, and performs no network request from its core entry point. Its one runtime side effect is the ΔT it installs in astronomy-engine, which keeps a single ΔT function for its whole module: each evaluation installs the ΔT of the instant it evaluates, and every entry point restores the engine's ΔT model when it returns, so a call leaves that model installed.

The engine's README and its crossing search's documentation say that a plain scan at a 5-day step loses both crossings when a Saturn station falls within 0.0103° of the target, or a Jupiter station within 0.0205°. A plain scan does lose such pairs, but the figures are twice the band. At the 12 Saturn and 11 Jupiter stations from 2019 to 2024 the engine's own longitudes turn with a second derivative of 1.61–1.78·10⁻³ °/day² for Saturn and 3.09–3.51·10⁻³ °/day² for Jupiter, so a 5-day scan can miss a pair only where the station is less than f″h²/8 past the target, 0.0050–0.0056° for Saturn and 0.0097–0.0110° for Jupiter; scanned at every phase of the 5-day grid, no Saturn pair 0.0103° deep and no Jupiter pair 0.0205° deep is missed. The engine audit's finding production-event-search-4, where the figures come from, gives the Saturn curvature as 1.64·10⁻³ °/day² but leaves out the half in the depth of the parabola. The 1.0.0 search's curvature test, which finds such turns, is not affected.

evidence.match: "rule": "a plain scan misses both crossings only when they fall inside one cell: depth < f″·h²/8"

evidence.anchor: production-event-search-4

resolution.note: The README and the crossing search's doc comment should give about 0.005° for Saturn and 0.010° for Jupiter, or the rule f″h²/8. F-89: statements in engine 1.0.0's README, NOTICE, LICENSING and doc comments that the claims ledger found inaccurate; correct them in the engine's next release, and the reference served here follows when it is regenerated for that release.

claims.statement: searchLongitudeCrossings(body, longitude, from, to, { stepDays, maxSamples }) makes the same longitude-crossing search as findLongitudeCrossings under a budget of ephemeris evaluations in which the root refinements count. A non-finite longitude from the ephemeris also throws RangeError. The crossing solver is tested on synthetic stations and on real stations of the engine's ephemeris, and is not proven complete.

evidence.match: throw new RangeError("Ephemeris returned a non-finite longitude.");

claims.statement: The crossing solver, which @zodiacs/engine/crossings exports as findLongitudeCrossingsWith and searchLongitudeCrossingsWith, takes the longitude function as its first argument and imports no ephemeris, so that entry point carries none; the root entry point exports the same two functions.
A DateInput string of the form YYYY-MM-DD is read as midnight UTC on that date of the proleptic Gregorian calendar.

Against JPL's DE440s at 20,000 instants from 1850 to 2150, the largest errors of the engine's declinations, rounded up to a tenth of an arcsecond, were 2.7″ for the Sun, 3.4″ for the Moon, 12.2″ for Mercury, 14.8″ for Venus, 14.6″ for Mars, 16.1″ for Jupiter, 21.6″ for Saturn, 19.3″ for Uranus, 15.5″ for Neptune and 4.6″ for Pluto. Within those errors the out-of-bounds flag can be wrong either way: at 2022-10-22T08:11:10.756Z the engine puts Mars 1.57″ inside the bound, where DE440s has it 1.05″ beyond.

chartDeclinations rotates each body's full ecliptic longitude and latitude into the true equator and equinox of date, using the chart's instant and the same ΔT as the chart, pinned or modelled. Its true obliquity, the IAU 2006 mean obliquity plus the IAU 2000B nutation in obliquity, equals ERFA's obl06 plus nut00b within the tests' tolerances (1e-9″ and 1e-10″); at 20,000 instants from 1850 to 2150 it was within 1.63 mas of obl06 plus nut06a (IAU 2000A), where astronomy-engine's five-term value, used until this change, was up to 85.6 mas from both.

No Swiss Ephemeris output was used to build the engine's ΔT table: its values are Table S15 of Stephenson, Morrison and Hohenkerk 2016 and the IERS and USNO observations it cites. With the birth instant known, that leaves the birthplace in an area about one degree of longitude wide (0.92° to 1.09°: about 110 km at the equator, 80 km at 45° and 55 km at 60°) and, from north to south, at least 400 km within 15° of the equator, 200 km within 45° and 70 km within 60° (a dense sweep of sidereal time at those edges found 464.9, 222.9 and 79.8 km); further from the equator it shrinks, to tens of kilometres in the far north, and near the Arctic Circle, where the ecliptic can lie along the horizon, the ascendant's degree can leave a strip less than a kilometre from north to south (0.84 km on the circle at 25.73° E on 21 December 1990, every match within a degree of latitude across the whole MC degree; 0.42 km at 174.3° W on 15 June 1990). A chart without a birth time is computed at 12:00 at the birthplace, an instant that depends on the place, so every code made from one carries the twelve bodies at 12:00 UTC on the civil birth date and no angles: every birthplace with that date gives the same code, which gives the date and nothing about the place. Unless the person shows birth details on the chart sheet, no image has a birth date, time, place or coordinates, a compatibility picture shows the names of the two charts and a group card shows the entered names or nicknames, and none shows more of a birth than its link. A chart is drawn from imageChart (through chart-image-sky for pattern and explorer images, and pictureBodies for two-chart pictures). With a birth time, the bodies and aspects are those at the UTC instant rounded to the whole minute, as the link carries them: before standard time the sheet's arcminute rows and aspect orbs had given the instant's seconds to 8 to 30 s and a blind solver the birthplace in strips 2.4 to 10 km wide, and a pattern's lossless orbs and the explorer's 0.001° gaps did the same; now every instant in the minute draws the same image. ASC, DSC, MC and IC sit at the middle of their whole degree, the angles a link carries, with whole-sign houses and no Placidus houses (on four births a solver's box went from 0.8 to 1.6 km by 3 to 57 km to at least 51 km by at least 186 km). Without a birth time, an image shows the sky at 12:00 UTC on the birth date, as the chart's link carries it, with the Moon's aspects left out, the same image for every birthplace on that date (the chart's own noon had given the instant to within half a minute through the Moon's orbs); the Moon card names the Moon's sign only when the Moon held it at every instant of that date in every time zone, from 00:00 at UTC+14 to 24:00 at UTC−12 (every offset since standard time lies in that span; the pinned history keeps two exceptions, dates kept across the date line in Alaska until 18 October 1867 and in the Philippines, Guam, Palau and much of Micronesia until the end of 1844, which began up to about an hour and a half earlier or ended up to about four and a quarter hours later), and the reading cards, which name only signs, are drawn the same way (on 28 September 2000 Mercury was in Libra at noon in Kathmandu and in Scorpio at noon in Pago Pago). A compatibility or composite picture draws each person the same way (a chart with a birth time at the whole minute, a chart without one computed here at 12:00 UTC on its date, and anyone without a birth time without the Moon) and finds the contacts again from what it draws: the page's composite midpoints, with the other chart known, had put a person's noon within about three and a half minutes, and the compatibility picture's Moon and its contacts within minutes. A solar or lunar return image, and its calendar file, is found from the natal Sun or Moon at the whole minute and gives the return to the whole minute (to the second or millisecond, from the exact birth instant, it had given the birth instant to under a second), with the angles at the middle of their whole degree and whole-sign houses only (the Ascendant to the arcminute had narrowed the latitude to 3 to 10 km); a solar return without a birth time is found from the Sun at 12:00 UTC on the birth date, the same for every birthplace (from noon at the birthplace it had given the UTC offset to half a second). The Big Three and rising cards, and the compatibility picture, print the rising sign's degree whole. Each image alone narrows a birthplace no more than a link does, but images shared together narrow it further: for a birth in Lyon in 1987 a link alone leaves about 19,100 km², a link and one solar return image cast at the birthplace, as return images are by default, about 3,900 km², about five times smaller, and a link with two solar return images and four lunar return images about 1,500 km².

claims.statement: The compute API's limits come from the measured cost of requests on one 4-core machine (Node 22.22.2, an Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz shared with other work, warm, through the handler with the bundled resolver). On @zodiacs/engine 0.1.1-rc.15, over every year from 1800 to 2199, an events request at the window limit (92 days, every body and kind) took CPU p50 165.7 ms, p95 244.0 ms and at most 359.2 ms, and positions at the instant limit (100 instants, every body) p50 66.0 ms, p95 93.5 ms and at most 170.1 ms, in the run with the higher maxima of two. Under the rules of 40 requests a minute per address, 10 of them events, one address can cost at most about 8.7 CPU-seconds a minute at those maxima (5.2 at the 95th percentiles); the other run gave 8.0 and the same sweep on rc.14 8.5. The engine calls the API makes cost between 2% and 7% more CPU time on rc.15 than on rc.14 on that machine. Through the packaged compatibility function, the first compute request in a fresh process took at most 266.2 ms, after an import of at most 72.8 ms (2026-09-29, rc.14). Measured again on 2026-10-05 on a 4-core machine (Node 22.22.2, an Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, each step started after two minutes in which no other process used more than a fifth of a CPU, at one-minute loads of 0.02 to 0.17), with the election search's costliest shapes beside the others, one engine after the other within the hour: at the maxima, 10 events and 30 positions requests a minute cost 10.7 CPU-seconds on rc.16 and 7.8 on rc.15 (6.8 and 5.9 at the 95th percentiles); the slowest elections request measured took 384 ms on rc.16, against 539 ms for the slowest events request. Two earlier runs on rc.16 that day, while the machine reported a 2.80 GHz processor and with earlier versions of the tool, gave 12.8 and 13.2 CPU-seconds a minute; in the one of them that timed elections requests the slowest took 489 ms, against 619 ms for events. At that time the API ran rc.17, whose bundle differed from rc.16's only in version strings and chunk comments; the rc.2 bundle has substantive changes, so the earlier measurements cannot stand in for a fresh sweep. Ten CPU-seconds a minute is the bound DECISIONS-2026-09-30 §7 set, and F-78 records rc.16's figure. The latency and cost the P3.3 gate asks for, on the deployed endpoints, are not yet recorded. A fresh rc.2 sweep on 2026-10-07 used the production handler’s TypeScript source and local-time bundle in one seeded interleaved run on Node 22.22.2, Xeon Platinum 8573C, under a four-CPU container quota: 4,600 requests across nine shapes after two warmups per shape. CPU maxima were events 1,001.5 ms, positions 287.1 ms, chart 15.7 ms, sky-fact 41.2 ms, time 24.1 ms; the four election shapes reached 1,129.6, 932.8, 1,447.5 and 1,008.4 ms respectively. The seven-endpoint API includes houses, which the nine-shape cost tool does not time. The current 40/10 rules give an illustrative 23.1 CPU-seconds per address per minute at these observed maxima, 9.2 at p95; neither is a universal cost bound. This run was sequential with respect to heavy builds/tests, but did not use the earlier two-minute quiet-load criterion; hardware and protocol differences prevent attributing the change to the engine. A separate 5,200-request houses sweep through the generated production bundle, all 13 systems in each year 1800–2199, measured CPU p95 23.0 ms and maximum 98.5 ms; it does not change the illustrative maximum rule arithmetic because positions remains costlier.

The Zodiacs sky-fact benchmark, version 0, published at /developers/sky-benchmark/v0/, is 300 questions, 60 in each of five families, drawn on 5 October 2026 from dates between 1900 and 2049, each asking for its answer in a fixed form: a sign, YES, NO or DEPENDS, or a date as YYYY-MM-DD. Its key is @zodiacs/engine 0.1.1-rc.16's longitudes and speeds, which are what positions() reports, and the Moon–Sun elongation of its moonPhase(), sampled every 10 minutes to 6 hours, depending on the body and the span searched, and narrowed to the second. A question is left out when a body is within 1′ of a sign boundary (the Moon 30′) at the instant asked about, when an event is within 10 minutes of the edge of a date or within the time the body takes to move 30″, more than the engine's largest measured longitude error for any body from 1900 to 2049 (20.4″ against Swiss Ephemeris, Venus, 2026), or when a station is within 6 hours of one; where the answer is that a planet stays in one sign on a date or enters a sign once in a period, also when a station is within 30″ of that sign's boundaries; when another entry of the body into the sign falls within those margins outside the period, for the Sun and the Moon as for the planets; and, for a lunation, when another of the same phase falls within 10 minutes outside it. A date with no time or zone is read from 14 hours before its midnight UTC to 36 hours after, with the compute API's own constants, and every date whose window holds an event is accepted; three DEPENDS answers turn only on offsets more than 10 hours from UTC. check_sky_fact gives the key's answer on all 300 questions and on 2,022 facts around them, among them every date that holds one of the 18 entries into a sign while retrograde in the ingress questions' periods; tool-answers.json holds its reply to each when v0 was drawn, unchanged, and those counts. The key and the tool read the same engine, so their agreement checks the tool's search, not the engine; every answer in the key also agrees with NASA JPL Horizons' apparent longitudes of date, sampled around each question. The four files are pinned by their bytes. The generator writes only a version not yet published, refuses to check v0 with one of its files missing or with an engine or ΔT tables other than those they name, and holds check_sky_fact's replies today to the published ones by their answers and the facts behind them, each event within 2 seconds, so a new engine or rule makes a new version. The scorer reads a reply strictly, its last non-empty line, and only when that fails leniently, the whole reply naming exactly one answer of the allowed kind; the lenient score is a rough guide. ΔT is observed to 24 September 2026, predicted to 2 October 2027 and extrapolated after that, and the engine's 1-σ estimate of its uncertainty reaches about 12 seconds by 2049.

At 2,000 instants from 1800 to 2199 they were within 0.4503″ and 0.4887″ of Swiss Ephemeris's SE_MEAN_NODE and SE_MEAN_APOG (docs/evidence/nutation-2026-09-29/results/swiss.json).

At a solstice the size of the Sun's declination differs from the true obliquity by exactly its ecliptic latitude, which stays within about 1.2″ of zero: computed with ERFA (IAU 2006/2000A), the real Sun is beyond the bound at 402 of the 800 solstices from 1800 to 2199, by up to 1.09″.

Before 1972 and after that table the instant is read as UT1, and TT = UT1 + ΔT from the engine's model zodiacs-deltat/1: Stephenson, Morrison & Hohenkerk 2016 (CC BY 4.0) up to 1941, then USNO and IERS observations, Bulletin A's predictions and a damped extrapolation, with a 1-σ band.
Both are counted in UTC milliseconds as JavaScript Date counts them, 86,400,000 to the day with no leap seconds; they are not ephemeris (TT) days.
Captured local resolution is checked arithmetically, without consulting the current timezone database or authenticating the historical claim.

Each is the definition Swiss Ephemeris uses, and every one agrees with Swiss's swe_houses_armc to within 0.0001″ given the same sidereal time, latitude and obliquity (Placidus, which iterates, to 0.01″).
Each resolution names the tzdb version, the transition behind the offset and its cause (dst, legal-change or date-line). docs/time.md describes every field.

Each sample installs its own ΔT, so every position and angle steps there together: the search finds each step inside the window from the engine's own arithmetic, splits at its millisecond and compares both sides.

End to end, from an instant read as UT1 as Swiss reads it, every system was within 0.055″ of Swiss's swe_houses_ex from 1850 to 2049, on a ladder of latitudes from 55° to 66.6° and on 3,000 draws within 66° of the equator (docs/evidence/nutation-2026-09-29/results/ladder.json); outside those years Swiss uses a long-term sidereal time of its own.

Every valid Date is accepted as input, but the ephemeris is evaluated only inside EPHEMERIS_SPAN: Terrestrial Time from 0001-04-30T12:00 to 3998-09-03T12:00, J2000 ± 730,000 days, the years astronomy-engine tabulates.
Every value is the engine's own at a millisecond, as natalChart computes it on UTC and the engine's time basis (not a pinned deltaT).
Existing Date values cannot reveal whether a caller previously normalized an invalid date; pass the original string when validation is needed.

From 1972 to 2027-10-02, TT = UTC + (TAI − UTC) + 32.184 s, with TAI − UTC from the IERS leap-second list of 2026-07-06 (it expires 2027-06-28; its last value is carried after that), and UT1 = UTC + (UT1 − UTC) from IERS: the EOP 20 C04 series in 1972, then finals2000A.all of 2026-09-24, observed then predicted.

Its dependency, astronomy-engine 2.1.19, ships ES modules in a package that does not declare "type": "module".

Measured against ERFA's IAU 2006/2000A chain applied to the same vectors at 4,001 instants from 1800 to 2200, that rotation puts a longitude at most 0.003691″ off, and the ascendant and midheaven at latitudes within 60° at most 0.006284″ and 0.003358″ off; with astronomy-engine's five-term nutation, used until this change, they were up to 0.2520″, 0.8235″ and 0.2457″ off (docs/evidence/nutation-2026-09-29/results/erfa-frame.json).

They are not covered by semantic-versioning guarantees; third-party code must use the documented entry points: the root, /calc, /geo, /houses, /sky, /techniques, /timing, /vedic, /window, /receipt, /crossings and /deltat.
They assume TT and UT1 run on continuously.
They do not establish the programme's 0.01″ physical declination target against Swiss Ephemeris.
This uses elapsed instants, not calendar anniversaries, local-time days or daylight-saving adjustments.
Those degenerate configurations are outside the verified angle scope.
Timezone identifiers are checked as nonempty strings, without requiring support in the current host's timezone database.
Unknown birth time does not establish a noon convention: an explicit 08:30 reference remains 08:30, while unavailable historical context remains unavailable.
Unknown strings, sparse slots, accessor slots, non-array iterables and simultaneous dst-gap/dst-fold claims reject with a RangeError that does not include supplied flag values.
Validation does not authenticate place facts, check that the advertised count equals all shards, or refresh a previously valid index when a shard changes independently.
Validation includes a constructed mapping to the existing JPL longitude fixture and a rounded published date-mapping example; neither establishes predictive validity.

What this version does not compute comes back as a typed refusal, such as gravitational deflection, or an instant whose UT1 or TT is outside 1800 to 2200: there calc has no comparison to take a bound from, while the root entry's functions still compute such an instant and flag it outside-reference-span.
Within them the flag can be wrong either way: at 2022-10-22T08:11:10.756Z the engine puts Mars 1.57″ inside the bound, where DE440s has it 1.05″ beyond.
YYYY-MM-DD, interpreted as midnight UTC using the proleptic Gregorian calendar.

A birth from before its place adopted a legal time uses the birthplace's own local mean time, worked out from its longitude, with the end of each zone's local mean time era taken from the same release.

A chart cites the engine's calculation receipt, which holds the instant as written, the coordinates and the settings, so its digest identifies the birth details: with the date and the place it gives back the time, and with the instant, which the positions give away, it gives back the place, even when the time is unknown; a comparison cites the adapter's own receipt, which holds nothing from either record, a place search the adapter's receipt, which holds nothing from the query, and the four compute tools the compute API's receipt, which holds no instant, date, zone or body from the request.
A chart without a birth time is shared as the positions at 12:00 UTC on the birth date, which give the date but nothing about the birthplace.

A chart's transit calendar is a file built on the device; the personal calendar feed, whose address carried the same code to the site's server, its cache and the subscriber's calendar service, was retired on 2026-10-03 and answers 410 Gone.
A code shared from such a chart carries the positions at 12:00 UTC on the birth date instead, so it gives nothing about the birthplace.

A date with no time or zone is read in every UTC offset in use today at once, from 14 hours before its midnight UTC to 36 hours after, so a body that changes sign or stations within those hours makes the answer DEPENDS, and every date that holds an event in one of those offsets is accepted.
A link to the playground carries a request only when the user chooses, after the #, which a browser never sends to a server.

A positions-only chart code has no name, date, time or place fields, but its exact positions give the birth date and the UTC birth time to the whole minute; its Ascendant and Midheaven are kept to the whole degree, which still narrows the birthplace to an area about one degree of longitude wide and, from north to south, at least 400 km within 15° of the equator, 200 km within 45° and 70 km within 60°, and near the Arctic Circle sometimes a strip less than a kilometre from north to south.
A received shared chart is not silently re-saved or re-shared as the recipient's own data.
A refusal is {"error": {"code", "message"}} with a stable code.

Check the consumed payload before calling it current: date is the UTC edition for today, planet, and sign files, with snapshotAt for their noon snapshot; upcoming events use from. generatedAt is a build timestamp and does not establish freshness.
Consumer calculator results do not depend on wallet ownership.
Cookieless analytics uses Plausible.
Current cache lifetimes are 300 seconds for sky/today.json, 3600 seconds for index.json, and 86400 seconds for other API files, including the other daily files and Markdown twins.

Daily files (publication scheduled from 00:00 UTC using positions computed for 12:00 UTC; delivery can be delayed): /api/v1/sky/today.json carries today's apparent geocentric tropical positions with formatted labels such as 14°53′ Virgo, moon phase and illumination, the active retrograde windows, the next new and full moon with signs and traditional names, the day's exact events, and a plain-language summary; /api/v1/sky/upcoming.json lists every lunation, sign ingress, station, eclipse, and exact aspect in the next 60 days plus the next occurrence of each kind and the current and next Mercury retrograde; /api/v1/planets/{sun|moon|mercury|…|pluto}.json gives one body's position, retrograde status and windows, and next ingress and station; /api/v1/signs.json gives the twelve signs with element, modality, rulers, computed Sun seasons, and current occupants.
Dates and positions should be cited with the page's displayed data horizon and UTC framing.

Draft specification, written for rc.3 to rc.6 (rc.7, rc.8, rc.15 and rc.16 each add a conventions set, listed in the changelog; rc.9 and rc.10 add house systems under rc.8's; rc.15's set records the instant's time scale and time basis; rc.16's adds the full IAU 2000B nutation and GeoMoon reduction): https://github.com/zodiacs-org/sdk/blob/fb57af7a2cd7c30983cc8fb655183d5a11f9cf30/docs/platform/receipt-draft-v1.md

Each chart records the ΔT it used, its one-sigma uncertainty, and the table's version and digest, and how its instant became UT1 and TT (timeScale); a chart outside 1800–2200 carries the outside-reference-span flag.
Each condition can be negated, every boundary is found to within a second, and the search is tested, not proven complete.
Each pairing combines written dynamics with element and modality facts and visible frequently asked questions.
Each question asks for its answer in a fixed form: a sign's name, YES, NO or DEPENDS, or a date as YYYY-MM-DD.
Each success carries result, receipt, backend and cite: cite.url is the endpoint's documentation and cite.receipt the SHA-256 of the receipt's RFC 8785 canonical JSON.

Each tool declares an output schema, and every result other than a refusal carries cite, as the compute API's answers do: cite.url is the tool's entry on the developer page and cite.receipt the SHA-256 of a receipt's RFC 8785 canonical JSON.

Eight tools: get_capabilities (versions, record schemas, request limits, the two resources, and what the adapter does not do), calculate_natal_chart, compare_calculation_records; three that run the compute API's own parsers and calculations without a zone, so that each returns the compute API's body for the same request: get_positions (up to 100 instants), find_events (sign ingresses, stations and new and full moons in a window of up to 92 days, by a search that is tested, not proven complete) and check_sky_fact (true, false or depends, with the values that decide it; a date is read as that day in every UTC offset in use today at once); resolve_birth_time, the compute API's time endpoint run with the zone histories built into the adapter (UTC and Terrestrial Time, with flags for skipped and repeated clock times, local mean time and a zone history before 1970 that the runtime's own time zone data disputes, and Julian dates up to 1923); and search_places, the site's birthplace search over GeoNames cities15000, under CC BY 4.0, built in as well.
Every calculation throws a RangeError for an instant outside Terrestrial Time 0001-04-30 to 3998-09-03, the years its ephemeris tabulates.
Every request uses store:false.

Files: https://zodiacs.org/developers/sky-benchmark/v0/items.json, https://zodiacs.org/developers/sky-benchmark/v0/key.json, https://zodiacs.org/developers/sky-benchmark/v0/tool-answers.json and https://zodiacs.org/developers/sky-benchmark/v0/scorer.mjs.

For chart and houses the receipt holds the instant and the coordinates, so cite.receipt identifies the birth details from either side: with the date and the place, trying times finds the time, and with the date and the time, trying places from a list of towns finds the place.
For daily deduplication, Plausible briefly processes the IP address and user agent to derive an identifier scoped to this site, device, and day.

For one of the 21 places of the Zodiacs time atlas, which records with citations what the clocks said in France and the United States from 1870 to 1919, it adds the atlas's reading of the same wall time, with the rule's uncertainty flag and citations and its distance from tzdb's instant.

From 1972 to 2027-10-02 a UTC birth time becomes Terrestrial Time through the IERS leap seconds, and the Earth's rotation (UT1) comes from IERS UT1 − UTC; other instants become Terrestrial Time through observed ΔT from IERS and US Naval Observatory records and the IERS predictions, within 0.09 s of the IERS value on every day from 1962.
GeoNames-derived place data is CC BY 4.0; downstream users must retain the package NOTICE.

Guide sends the questions you type, recent Guide messages, and enabled public page or sky context to our cloud service.
Historical civil time from 1970 on uses the IANA/ICU history supplied by the visitor's browser or device runtime.
Holding a Zodiac is optional context; it does not make a chart more accurate, a person more compatible, or an interpretation more authoritative.
Install, privacy, limits and uninstall: https://zodiacs.org/developers/mcp/

It also carries the IANA time zone history before 1970 and the IERS leap-second list, both public domain, a UT1 − UTC table derived from IERS series, and catalogue values for the stars of the Vedic ayanamsas; the package NOTICE names each source, and LICENSING.md gives their terms and three questions about them that are still open.
It also reads a date written in the Julian calendar up to 1923, and with a country code gives the birth forms' note on when that country changed calendar.
It computes apparent geocentric tropical positions, natal charts, transits, synastry, lunar phase, and Saturn-return seasons.
It does not automatically attach your saved birth chart or personal chart placements.
It does not store the raw IP or user agent; the salt rotates and is deleted every 24 hours.
It is an unpublished candidate distributed as a digest-pinned archive, and it is not on npm.
It is browser-first, Node-compatible, ESM-only and synchronous, with separate entry points.
It is not sent to OpenAI or included in provider metadata.
It marks the Moon's sign as unverified, because the Moon can change sign during that local date.
It omits the rising sign, angles, and houses.
It opens no listener and no port, and the calculation runs on the user's own machine; what an assistant connected to it then does with a result is a separate question the adapter cannot control.
It performs no astrology calculation and bundles no ephemeris or place data.
It preserves requested versus actual houses, unknown-time reference instants and supplied provenance; it does not authenticate claims or recalculate positions.
It recomputes each citation's digest with the browser's own SHA-256 and shows the request in cURL, JavaScript, Python, Swift and Ruby, each with its standard library.

Its Markdown twin, https://zodiacs.org/developers/playground.md, lists every request with a cURL command and its documented citation digest, and https://zodiacs.org/developers/playground/examples.json holds each request with its documented answer.
Its facts are a body's sign, a retrograde, an ingress, a lunar phase, and one of the five major aspects between two bodies, held within the orb the chart endpoint uses for that aspect.
Its npm tarball is byte-identical to the vendored archive.
Keep birth inputs in the browser.
Licensing chain: the engine uses MIT-licensed Astronomy Engine and explicitly excludes Swiss Ephemeris code. @zodiacs/engine/geo contains adapters, not a bundled place database.
Life Path meanings for 1 to 9, 11, 22, and 33 live under https://zodiacs.org/numerology/life-path/{number}/. https://zodiacs.org/numerology/ All calculators and calendars: https://zodiacs.org/tools/
Markdown twins exist at /api/v1/sky/today.md and /api/v1/sky/upcoming.md.
Methodology and accuracy notes: https://zodiacs.org/methodology/
No assistant has been scored on it yet.

OpenAI states that API data is not used to train its models by default; its abuse-monitoring logs keep submitted content for up to 30 days, or longer where the law requires it or where that is needed to protect its services or others from harm.
Operations and schemas: https://zodiacs.org/api/v1/openapi.json (tag compute).
Optional @zodiacs/engine/receipt validates a Zodiacs-owned draft natal envelope from a fresh full public Chart.
Pair pages support questions about a specific pairing; the calculator is better when exact birth details are available. https://zodiacs.org/compatibility/

Per-year files cover retrograde windows (with station instants and signs, shadow boundaries, and clippedStart/clippedEnd flags where the scan boundary truncated a window), stations, sign ingresses, moon phases, eclipses, and exact aspects.
Placidus and Koch fall back to whole sign inside the polar circle, where the absolute latitude is 90° minus the obliquity or more, and return the polar-fallback flag.
Plain Node needs 20.19.0 or a later 20.x, or 22.7.0 or later; bundlers are not affected.
Planet positions are apparent geocentric tropical longitudes produced with Astronomy Engine.

Planets: the ten commonly used astrological planets, their symbols, themes, rulerships, and orbital context. https://zodiacs.org/learn/planets/ Houses: all twelve houses, including angularity, modality, and the life topics each house traditionally covers. https://zodiacs.org/learn/houses/ Aspects: conjunction, sextile, square, trine, and opposition, with angle, orb, and interpretive function. https://zodiacs.org/learn/aspects/ Placements: all 120 planet-in-sign combinations at /learn/placements/{planet}-in-{sign}/, with classical dignity and computed transit windows. https://zodiacs.org/learn/placements/ Rising-sign profiles: all twelve ascendants at /rising-sign/{sign}/, including traditional chart rulers and modern co-rulers where they differ. https://zodiacs.org/rising-sign/ Birthday astrology: one page for every calendar date at /birthday/{month}-{day}/, with the Sun sign checked across 1940–2030, degree spans, decans, and year-by-year cusp tables. https://zodiacs.org/birthday/

Separately cached files may differ from index.json.coverage.dailyDate.
Seven endpoints under https://zodiacs.org/api/v1/ calculate from a JSON body sent with POST, on the same @zodiacs/engine 1.0.0 with astronomy-engine 2.1.19.
Share links keep chart data in the URL fragment, which is not sent in normal HTTP requests, and the links the site makes now carry none in their query string.
Since rc.12 it also computes secondary progressions, and, as separate functions since rc.11, aspects under a configurable policy and declinations with parallels.

Since rc.15 a chart reads its instant from 1972 to 2027-10-02 as UTC: TT from the IERS leap-second list, and UT1 from IERS UT1 − UTC (EOP 20 C04 in 1972, finals2000A.all from 1973-01-02), reported as ΔT model iers-utc/1.

Since rc.15 two separate entry points add Hellenistic timing (@zodiacs/engine/timing: profections, firdaria, zodiacal releasing, solar arc directions) and the sidereal zodiac with Jyotish techniques (@zodiacs/engine/vedic: ayanamsas, sidereal charts, nakshatras, vargas, KP sub-lords, dashas); the root imports neither, and this site uses neither.

Source lines identify Astronomy Engine, the NASA eclipse catalog where applicable, and the IANA time-zone database.
Symbolic traits should be framed as optional emphasis, never rank or superiority.
The SDK can support Zodiac shelves, identity receipts, chart overlays, compatibility context, seasonal moments, share cards, profiles, and opted-in AI astrology context.
The SDK provides verified inputs; each app owns its interpretive copy and rendering.

The Zodiacs sky-fact benchmark, version 0, is 300 questions about the sky that a calculation settles, drawn on 5 October 2026 from dates between 1900 and 2049: the sign of a body at an instant given to the minute in UTC, the sign of a body on a date, whether a planet was retrograde on a date, the date a body entered a sign, and the date of a new moon, first quarter, full moon or last quarter, 60 of each.
The Zodiacs.org site specifically resolves 12:00 local civil time for this case and marks the Moon's sign as unverified.

The answer key comes from @zodiacs/engine 0.1.1-rc.16, sampled every 10 minutes to 6 hours and narrowed to the second, and every answer in it agrees with NASA JPL Horizons. check_sky_fact gives the key's answer on every question, and its replies are published beside the key; the key and the tool read the same engine, so this checks the tool's search, not the engine.
The birth chart, compatibility, moon sign, rising sign, moon phase, Saturn return, transit, and baby-zodiac tools calculate in the visitor's browser.
The calculation suite is tested against NASA JPL Horizons reference values: at the two dates checked, 1907 and 2020, the largest difference is 14.8 arcseconds (Neptune, 2020).
The calendar pages print computed values in visible HTML.

The chart endpoint (/chart) returns bodies, angles, house cusps and aspects for a place and an instant, given in UTC or as a local time in an IANA zone, in any of the engine's thirteen house systems; /houses returns the angles and cusps alone, and /positions the positions and speeds of chosen bodies at up to 100 instants.
The core entry makes no network request.

The core package accepts UTC rather than inventing an unknown birth instant: an integrating app should choose and disclose its reference instant, pass timeKnown: false, and treat all returned body degrees as reference positions.
The current web Guide conversation stays in the browser session, is not account-synced, and is not stored as text by Zodiacs.org.
The displayed degrees remain noon-reference positions, not claims about an unknown birth instant.

The elections endpoint (/elections) returns the stretches of a window of up to 31 days in which up to five conditions all hold: the Moon waxing or waning; the Moon void of course, from its last exact Ptolemaic aspect in a sign to the Sun or a planet from Mercury to Pluto until it enters the next sign; a body in a sign; a planet retrograde; and a body in the 1st, 4th, 7th or 10th house at a place within 60° of the equator.
The events endpoint (/events) lists sign ingresses, stations and new and full moons in a window of up to 92 days, found by the engine's crossing search, which is tested, not proven complete.
The files are dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0.

The function writes nothing from a request or its result to a log, a file or a database, responses carry Cache-Control: no-store, and the rate-limit check sends Vercel's firewall the request's headers, never its body.
The generated draft reply is sent back to OpenAI for a second safety check before it is shown.
The in-document Powered by Zodiacs.org link is required and cannot be removed, relabeled, or redirected.
The package does not send them anywhere, so an app that only needs a calculation needs no server for it.
The package's licence expression is MIT AND CC-BY-4.0: its code is MIT, and the 32 ΔT values from Stephenson, Morrison and Hohenkerk's Table S15 in its ΔT module are CC BY 4.0.
The registry read of 2026-10-11 records 1.0.0 under latest and rc.16, an earlier candidate, under next.
The required sandbox is allow-scripts allow-forms allow-same-origin allow-popups allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox.

The scorer's strict reading, which gives the benchmark's score, takes a reply's last line; beside it, a lenient score, a rough guide, also accepts a reply that names exactly one answer of the allowed kind anywhere.
The site saved-chart/account format is unchanged, and the standalone starter retains its separately pinned engine rc.3.
The site's own calculators do not use it.

The sky-fact endpoint (/sky-fact) answers whether a stated fact holds at an instant or on a date, true, false or depends, with the computed values that decide it; depends means the answer turns on the time of day or on the zone.

The time endpoint (/time) reads a local civil time with @zodiacs/engine/geo, the resolver the birth chart calculator uses, and returns UTC, Terrestrial Time and ΔT, with flags for skipped and repeated clock times, local mean time, and a zone history before 1970 that the server's own time zone data disputes.
There are no cookies, storage, wallet APIs, signing, transactions, or third-party analytics in the package.
There is no key.
They also publish Schema.org Dataset and Event nodes so the dated facts remain machine-readable.

Thirteen house systems are supported, each as Swiss Ephemeris defines it: whole sign, Placidus, Koch, Porphyry, Regiomontanus, Campanus, Topocentric (Polich–Page), Alcabitius, Equal (Ascendant), Equal-MC, Vehlow, Meridian (axial rotation) and Morinus.
This establishes distribution and provenance, not numerical accuracy or deployed site/MCP adoption.
This site does not use it.
Two resources, zodiacs://conventions and zodiacs://methodology, give the conventions vocabulary of its records and how it calculates.
Unused table-building calls are marked pure, since 1.0.0-rc.2, so bundlers can drop the tables a program does not read; exported tables are frozen.
Verified SLSA provenance binds release.yml, engine commit f8992a4c1dfedd9e69c0783e2c185e22580460f7 and release run 38144970198; npm audit signatures verifies the attestation.
Version 0's files will not change: a new engine or rule makes a new version.
When birth time is unknown, the Zodiacs.org site uses 12:00 local civil time as a reference for body positions.

Account sync is an opt-in transmission.

Astronomical accuracy tests validate position calculations, not astrology as science; interpretations are traditional and reflective, not scientifically validated predictions.

Numerical: each value is computed by two independent routes (cross-product intersections, and the pole-height or projection formulas) and checked against its defining property with ERFA coordinate routines (s2c, rx, c2s, hd2ae); over this arbiter's 22 vectors the largest disagreement is 7.3e-10″.

An instant is ISO 8601 with Z or a numeric offset, to the second or the millisecond: 2026-09-29T08:15:00Z or 1990-06-15T14:30:00+02:00.

As posições planetárias são calculadas com um mecanismo astronômico e comparadas com dados de referência do JPL da NASA, com margem de poucos centésimos de grau.

Mudanças históricas de horário a partir de 1970 são resolvidas com o histórico IANA fornecido pelo navegador ou pelo sistema do dispositivo, e as anteriores com uma versão fixa do banco de dados IANA, incluindo os registros antigos que ele mantém à parte para lugares cujos relógios depois passaram a coincidir com os de outra cidade, que seus mantenedores consideram menos confiáveis.
Sem o horário, usamos 12:00 no horário civil local como referência para as posições e omitimos ascendente, ângulos e casas.

A calculadora usa 12:00 como referência, deixa de fora o ascendente e as casas em vez de inventá-los e marca o signo lunar como não verificado até você informar um horário, porque a Lua pode mudar de signo ao longo do dia.
A data em que a hora média local de cada lugar terminou vem dos registros históricos completos do banco de dados IANA (versão 2025c).
Dessa data até 1970, a hora legal, incluindo as mudanças de relógio durante guerras, vem da mesma versão do banco de dados IANA.

O Guide envia cada pergunta à OpenAI; se você pressionar “Anexar meu mapa”, que só é oferecido na prévia da sincronização criptografada, um resumo apenas das posições acompanha cada mensagem enquanto “Usando meu mapa” estiver ativo.
O mecanismo é testado com dados de referência do JPL Horizons da NASA.
Os testes com o JPL validam o cálculo das posições astronômicas, não a interpretação astrológica.
Para nascimentos a partir de 1970, convertemos seu horário local com o histórico de fusos horários IANA disponível no navegador ou no sistema do dispositivo, incluindo o horário de verão.

Por exemplo, no histórico do navegador, um nascimento em Estocolmo ao meio-dia de 1º de julho de 1947 corresponde a 10:00 UTC, com o horário de verão de Berlim, embora a Suécia usasse +1:00; o mapa usa 11:00.
Se você entrar em uma conta, seus mapas salvos e os dados de nascimento deles são enviados para a sua conta no Supabase, protegidos por segurança em nível de linha.

Se você não souber a hora de nascimento, usamos 12:00 no horário civil local como referência para as posições; omitimos ascendente, ângulos e casas e marcamos o signo da Lua como não verificado, porque a Lua pode mudar de signo durante o dia.

Um link, calendário, convite ou cartão compartilhado a partir de um mapa assim leva as posições das 12:00 UTC da data de nascimento, porque o meio-dia no local de nascimento revelaria o fuso horário dele ou, antes da hora padrão, a longitude.

Esta calculadora usa uma versão fixa do histórico de horários IANA para nascimentos antes de 1970 e, a partir daí, o histórico IANA/ICU fornecido pelo navegador ou pelo sistema do dispositivo, e mostra o instante UTC calculado para você conferir.

A OpenAI informa que, por padrão, os dados da API não são usados para treinar seus modelos e que seus registros de monitoramento de abuso guardam o conteúdo enviado por até 30 dias, ou por mais tempo quando a lei exige ou quando isso é necessário para proteger seus serviços ou outras pessoas contra danos.

Armazenamos seu endereço de e-mail e todos os mapas salvos no seu navegador enquanto você está conectado, inclusive os salvos antes de você entrar, com os respectivos dados de nascimento, no nosso provedor de banco de dados, o Supabase, para que eles possam aparecer nos seus outros dispositivos.

As posições planetárias de um mapa são as da hora de nascimento em UTC arredondada ao minuto inteiro, que ainda indicam a data e a hora de nascimento até o minuto; o ascendente e o Meio do Céu aparecem apenas em graus inteiros, e as casas Placidus ficam de fora.
Cada verificação de cota posterior apaga as contagens mais antigas que o dia UTC anterior e os registros de solicitação com mais de 48 horas.

Если время неизвестно, мы используем 12:00 местного гражданского времени как ориентир для положений и не показываем асцендент, углы и дома.

Исторические изменения часов с 1970 года берутся из истории IANA, предоставленной браузером или системой устройства, а более ранние — из зафиксированного выпуска базы IANA вместе со старыми записями, которые база хранит отдельно для мест, чьи часы позже совпали с часами другого города; её составители считают эти записи менее надёжными.
Положения планет рассчитываются астрономическим движком и сверяются с эталонными данными NASA JPL с точностью до сотых долей градуса.
Время событий указывается в UTC, положения — в градусах тропического зодиака.

Калькулятор берёт 12:00 как ориентир, не показывает асцендент и дома, чтобы не придумывать их, и помечает лунный знак как неподтверждённый, пока вы не укажете время: Луна может сменить знак в течение дня.

Guide отправляет каждый вопрос в OpenAI; если вы согласитесь прикрепить карту (это доступно только в предварительной версии зашифрованной синхронизации), к каждому сообщению добавляется сводка только с положениями, пока прикрепление включено.
Дату, когда в каждом месте закончилось местное среднее время, мы берём из полных исторических записей базы IANA (выпуск 2025c).
Движок сверяется с эталонными данными NASA JPL Horizons.
Для рождений с 1970 года местное время переводится по истории часовых поясов IANA, доступной браузеру или системе устройства, с летним временем.

Если время рождения неизвестно, мы используем 12:00 местного гражданского времени как ориентир для положений, не показываем асцендент, углы и дома и отмечаем знак Луны как непроверенный, потому что за день Луна может сменить знак.
Если вы войдёте в аккаунт, сохранённые карты вместе с данными рождения загружаются в ваш аккаунт Supabase и защищены политиками доступа на уровне строк.
Например, в полдень 1 июля 1947 года рождение в Стокгольме в истории браузера приходится на 10:00 UTC по летнему времени Берлина, хотя Швеция жила по времени +1:00, и карта использует 11:00.
От этой даты до 1970 года законное время, включая военные изменения часов, берётся из того же выпуска базы IANA.
Сверка с JPL подтверждает расчёт астрономических положений, а не астрологическую интерпретацию.

Ссылка, календарь, приглашение или карточка, которыми делятся из такой карты, содержат положения на 12:00 UTC в дату рождения, потому что полдень в месте рождения выдал бы его часовой пояс или, до введения поясного времени, долготу.
Индикатор в начале страницы считает её прямо на вашем устройстве: показывает название текущей фазы, процент освещённости, знак Луны и время UTC.

Этот калькулятор использует зафиксированный выпуск истории часов IANA для рождений до 1970 года и историю IANA, доступную браузеру или системе устройства, для более поздних, а рассчитанный момент UTC показывается для проверки.
Plausible не получает данных рождения, публичного адреса, идентификатора карты, идентификатора подключённого аккаунта или точного списка знаков, которыми владеет адрес.
Supabase обрабатывает записи аккаунта и базы данных, а Vercel выполняет серверный слой, который их проверяет и шифрует.

Для карты без времени рождения они содержат полдень в месте рождения, что выдаёт его часовой пояс или, до введения поясного времени, его долготу, а изображение двух карт, сделанное с таким кодом, рисует эту карту по этим положениям, а не по небу на 12:00 UTC.
Доступ к аккаунту ограничен защитой на уровне строк, а Supabase шифрует данные при хранении.

Если вы отдельно выберете Keep this on every device (хранить на всех устройствах), дата и точность времени записи, категория, заметка, зафиксированный прогноз и идентификатор карты отправляются в Supabase и хранятся для аккаунта, в который вы вошли.
Затем сгенерированный черновик ответа снова передаётся OpenAI для второй проверки безопасности, прежде чем вы его увидите.
Каждая следующая проверка лимита удаляет счётчики старше предыдущего дня по UTC и записи запросов старше 48 часов.

Карта без времени рождения нарисована по небу на 12:00 UTC в дату рождения, как и её ссылка, что выдаёт дату, но ничего не говорит о месте рождения; знак Луны показан, только если Луна пробыла в нём весь этот день повсюду, а изображение двух карт не показывает Луну такого человека.
Когда вы отправляете вопрос Guide, это сообщение, недавние сообщения Guide и видимый контекст Guide передаются OpenAI для проверки безопасности входящего текста и для создания черновика ответа.
Мы не передаём этот идентификатор OpenAI и не помещаем текст переписки в метаданные поставщика.
Мы считаем просмотры страниц и анонимное использование функций с помощью Plausible — сервиса аналитики без файлов cookie.

По заявлению OpenAI, данные API по умолчанию не используются для обучения её моделей, а её журналы мониторинга злоупотреблений хранят отправленное содержимое до 30 дней или дольше, если этого требует закон или если это нужно, чтобы защитить её сервисы или других от вреда.

Пока вы в аккаунте, мы храним ваш адрес электронной почты и все карты, сохранённые в вашем браузере, включая сохранённые до входа, вместе с их данными рождения у нашего поставщика базы данных, Supabase, чтобы они могли появляться на других ваших устройствах.

Положения планет в карте взяты на момент рождения по UTC, округлённый до целой минуты, и всё равно выдают дату и время рождения с точностью до минуты; асцендент и середина неба показаны только с точностью до целого градуса, а дома Плацидуса не показаны.
Положения планет в нём всё равно позволяют определить дату и время вашего рождения с точностью до минуты: они взяты на момент рождения по UTC, округлённый до целой минуты.
У карты без времени рождения нет асцендента и середины неба, и её код содержит небо на 12:00 UTC в дату рождения, что выдаёт дату, но ничего не говорит о месте рождения.

Чтобы не считать одно и то же устройство несколько раз за день, Plausible кратковременно обрабатывает IP-адрес и user agent и выводит из них идентификатор, ограниченный этим сайтом, устройством и днём.
Чтобы ограничить повторные вступления, мы также храним односторонний код, полученный из вашего IP-адреса; он удаляется по окончании следующего дня по UTC.
Это не сквозное шифрование: Zodiacs.org и Supabase технически могут обрабатывать сохранённую запись, чтобы обеспечивать синхронизацию, поддержку, экспорт и удаление.
